What Is AIS?
Why Does It Matter for Cable Security?

Article Series 02 • AIS • Dark Vessel Detection • SAR Satellite

SERIES → 01 Submarine Cable 02 AIS 03 Taiwan Status 04 Threats 05 Enforcement 06 Methodology
Imagine this rule: every vehicle on the highway must broadcast its license plate number, current position, speed, and destination to the entire world every few seconds.

That's exactly the rule at sea — for large vessels. The system is called AIS. Until someone secretly switches off the broadcaster.

AIS: The Ship's Digital Passport

AIS (Automatic Identification System) is a radio transponder installed on vessels that automatically broadcasts ship information via VHF radio. Under the IMO's SOLAS convention, all ocean-going vessels over 300 gross tons and all passenger ships are required to have AIS installed and activated.

AIS broadcasts every few seconds, allowing nearby vessels, port authorities, coast guards, and global satellite networks to track the ship's real-time position.

What Does AIS Broadcast?

Data FieldDescriptionExample
MMSIMaritime Mobile Service Identity (9 digits, like a national ID)416123456
Vessel NameRegistered ship nameXING SHUN 39
Call SignRadio communication identifierVRCS7
IMO NumberPermanent IMO identifier (theoretically unchangeable)9876543
Vessel TypeCargo, tanker, fishing, passenger, etc.Cargo
Flag StateEncoded in first 3 digits of MMSI (MID code)Tanzania (677)
Lat / LonGPS position, ~10m accuracy25.12°N 121.8°E
SOGSpeed over ground (knots)4.2 kn
COGCourse over ground (degrees)185°
DestinationManually entered by crew — may be inaccurateKAOHSIUNG

This information is itself valuable intelligence. Vessel type, flag state, speed, and heading can all be used to identify anomalous behavior. This site collects exactly this data.

AIS's Fatal Flaw: Anyone Can Turn It Off

The biggest problem with AIS is that it's entirely voluntary broadcasting — nobody can force a ship to keep its signal on. Any crew member can make a vessel disappear from all AIS tracking platforms in a few button presses.

This is called "going dark" in the industry. Going dark isn't necessarily illegal — there are legitimate reasons for a captain to disable AIS, such as for safety in piracy-prone areas. But in Taiwan's surrounding waters, a vessel suddenly disabling AIS while approaching a submarine cable route is a very serious warning signal.

Beyond switching off, AIS can also be spoofed — vessels can broadcast false position coordinates, fake speeds, or even another vessel's identity. This "AIS Spoofing" is an item our scoring system specifically monitors.

Why Do Vessels "Go Dark"?

🐟
Illegal FishingConcealing cross-border fishing or operations in restricted zones, avoiding detection by fisheries management authorities.
🛢️
Sanctions EvasionCountries under international sanctions (Russia, North Korea, Iran) use "shadow fleets" to transship goods, switching off AIS to hide cargo movements.
🔄
Ship-to-Ship (STS) TransferConducting cargo transfers at sea while disabling AIS to avoid port inspections — common in oil smuggling.
🔌
Submarine Cable SabotageDisabling AIS before approaching a cable to avoid real-time tracking and interception during a sabotage operation — exactly the pattern of Xing Shun 39 in January 2025.
🔍
Maritime ReconnaissanceIntelligence-gathering vessels operating in sensitive waters switch off AIS to conceal their surveillance intent.
Our observation: On January 11, 2025, Xing Shun 39 disabled its AIS approximately 10 km from the Taiwan-Asia-US cable route, before the cable was confirmed severed. This "go dark before approaching the cable" pattern is one of the key behaviors our threat-scoring system is designed to detect.

SAR Satellites: Eyes in the Dark

Going dark on AIS doesn't mean a vessel has disappeared — only that it's vanished from conventional tracking systems. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites can detect any metallic object on the water surface via radar scanning, completely unaffected by weather, cloud cover, or time of day.

The SAR data used by this site comes from Global Fishing Watch, which scans Taiwan's surrounding waters via SAR satellites and cross-references detected vessel positions against AIS data:

  • SAR-detected vessel + has AIS signal → Normal
  • SAR-detected vessel + no AIS signal → Dark Vessel

These "dark vessels" become priority monitoring targets. A vessel detected by SAR near a submarine cable route with no AIS signal immediately triggers high-level alertness.

Identity Manipulation: More Cunning Than Going Dark

Some vessels go further — not just disabling AIS, but frequently changing their name, call sign, or even falsely reporting their IMO number to create identity confusion. This behavior itself is a major red flag.

Shadow Fleet Identity Manipulation Tactics Based on case analysis in our research, typical shadow vessels will:
  • Frequently change flags between ports (e.g., Tanzania → Togo → Cameroon)
  • Change vessel names to disconnect old tracking records from new identities
  • Conceal actual ship owners through layers of offshore shell companies
  • Conduct ship-to-ship (STS) transfers to move cargo, avoiding port inspections
This site's Identity Tracking feature is specifically designed to detect such frequent identity-change anomalies.

AIS and Submarine Cables: Connecting All the Dots

Now we can see the clear logical chain:

  1. AIS tells us where every large vessel is and what it's doing
  2. When a vessel "goes dark" or uses AIS spoofing, we find it via SAR satellites
  3. We cross-reference vessel positions against Taiwan's submarine cable routes
  4. If a vessel goes dark near a cable, loiters at low speed, or shows anomalous navigation patterns, its threat score rises
  5. Vessels reaching the score threshold are flagged as "suspicious" and listed on this site

This logic is the core of our monitoring system. For the full scoring methodology, see Article 06: Our Methodology.

Two Ways AIS Is Received: Terrestrial vs Satellite

An AIS signal has to be received before it can be "seen." Understanding the two ways it is received is what separates real "going dark" from a mere coverage gap.

📻
Terrestrial AISCoastal base stations receive VHF signals with real-time updates and high accuracy, but because of the Earth's curvature their effective range is usually only ~40–70 nautical miles. The farther offshore, the sparser the coverage.
🛰️
Satellite AIS (S-AIS)Low-orbit satellites receive from space and cover the open ocean, but a satellite must pass overhead to hear a signal, so updates have gaps; in busy waters overlapping signals can also be missed.

This matters for monitoring: when a ship vanishes beyond terrestrial range, between satellite passes, it may have genuinely switched off AIS (gone dark) — or it may just be in a coverage hole. Telling the two apart requires independent SAR satellite detection, which is exactly why this site cross-references AIS "going dark" with SAR dark-vessel hits.

Class A vs Class B Large merchant ships are required to use higher-power, more frequently updating Class A units; many small craft and fishing boats use cheaper, lower-power Class B. Class B signals are weaker and more easily missed, so "no AIS" does not always mean "deliberately dark" — vessel type and equipment class must be weighed in any assessment.

FAQ

Is AIS mandatory?
Under the IMO SOLAS convention, all ocean-going vessels over 300 gross tons and all passenger ships must install and activate AIS, broadcasting vessel information every few seconds.
Is turning off AIS illegal?
Not necessarily. There are legitimate reasons (e.g. piracy-prone areas) to disable AIS. But going dark for no reason near a submarine cable in Taiwan's waters is a serious warning signal.
How do you track "dark vessels" with no AIS signal?
Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites detect metallic objects on the water surface, which are cross-referenced against AIS. A vessel seen by SAR but with no AIS signal is flagged as a dark vessel.
What is AIS spoofing?
A vessel broadcasting false position coordinates, fake speeds, or even another ship's identity to conceal its true movements. It is one of the behaviors our threat-scoring system specifically detects.
